title: SYSK’s Fall True Crime Playlist: The Tylenol Murders, Part II
summary: Part two of the Tylenol murders episode (1982 Chicago cyanide-laced Extra Strength Tylenol killings). Covers Johnson & Johnson's crisis response and recall, the Silver/Golden Anvil PR awards, tamper-resistant packaging changes, cotton and caplet history, congressional and FDA responses, the first named suspect Roger Arnold and the mistaken-identity killing of John Stanisha, the extortion suspect James Lewis (alias Robert Richardson) and the DNA reinvestigation, victims' families' views, the 1985 Diane Elsroth death, and a 2011 self-published book alleging a cover-up. Ends with a listener anecdote about synthetic farts.

segments.title: Cold open
segments.summary: Josh previews part two of the 1982 Chicago Tylenol murders episode, covering suspects and the lack of charges.

segments.title: Opening banter and show intro
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the show and the episode, recapping that seven people died in 1982 from cyanide-laced Tylenol.

segments.title: Johnson & Johnson's crisis response and recall
segments.summary: Johnson & Johnson initially resisted a large recall until Mayor Jane Byrne called for one. The company recalled Chicago bottles, then all extra strength Tylenol nationally (about 31 million bottles, roughly $100 million), and later received a Silver Anvil and Golden Anvil for its crisis handling, while McNeil Consumer Products, a subsidiary, makes the pills. The hosts also discuss a separate Detroit-area Ballpark Franks razor blade scare.

segments.title: Recall costs and public trust
segments.summary: Discussion of the recall as a sacrifice to restore trust, along with a $100,000 reward and hotline that went unclaimed.

segments.title: Victim framing and old packaging
segments.summary: Johnson & Johnson was portrayed as a victim, helping regain trust. The hosts describe pre-1982 packaging with no tamper seal and cotton stuffing.

segments.title: Tampering fears and domestic terrorism
segments.summary: Tampering was easy then across many products. The poisoning is considered an early domestic terrorism incident, and fear spread to milk and cereal, illustrated by flight attendant Paula Prince's coworker.

segments.title: Tamper-resistant packaging and Tylenol Murders Act
segments.summary: Within six weeks Tylenol introduced three-part tamper-resistant packaging and caplets. Congress passed the Tylenol bill in 1983 making such tampering a federal offense, and the FDA set guidelines in 1989. Other manufacturers followed.

segments.title: Spread of tamper-proof packaging
segments.summary: Other consumer products like soap began adopting tamper-evident packaging.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Psychological profile of the killer
segments.summary: A profile described a Jekyll-and-Hyde man in his twenties or thirties, possibly suicidal after the killings, per a Cook County medical examiner's speculation. No one was ever charged.

segments.title: Task force and leads
segments.summary: The Tylenol Task Force of 140 people received thousands of calls, and about 1,200 leads were deemed worth checking. Staff was cut to 40 by late October and 20 by year end.

segments.title: Lack of motive and surveillance
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how easy it was to tamper in stores in 1982 without cameras or credit card trails, and the lack of a motive.

segments.title: Suspect Roger Arnold and John Stanisha killing
segments.summary: Roger Arnold, a 49-year-old dockhand who studied chemistry, was an early named suspect; police found a poison handbook, five unregistered guns, and his admission of past cyanide. He was cleared, but later shot John Stanisha, a computer consultant, by mistake while targeting a bar owner, Marty Sinclair. Arnold served 15 of 30 years and died nine years after release.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Suspect James Lewis and the extortion letter
segments.summary: A letter demanding $1 million was sent to Johnson & Johnson, traced to a closed Chicago travel agency. The name Robert Richardson was an alias for James Lewis, who had a past of credit card fraud and a murder charge in Kansas City. Lewis admitted writing the letter but denied poisoning, and during an interview described how he would have done it.

segments.title: Lewis arrest and cases cleared
segments.summary: Lewis was found in New York Public Library and sentenced for extortion and fraud, serving 13 years. Investigators could not place him in Chicago on the day of the killings. In 2009 the FBI sought DNA and fingerprints, which the Lewises contested in court before giving samples, with no result reported.

segments.title: Ongoing cold case and DNA hopes
segments.summary: The case remains unsolved. A fingerprint and DNA from bottles exist, and police sergeant Scott Winkelmann believes it is solvable. The hosts mention Ted Kaczynski being cleared by DNA.

segments.title: Victims' families
segments.summary: Families of victims, including Monica Janis and Joseph Manus, describe lasting trauma. Michelle Rosen, daughter of Mary Reiner, disputes the lone-poisoner theory and suspects a supply chain issue and cover-up.

segments.title: 1985 Diane Elsroth death and capsule bans
segments.summary: In 1985 Diane Elsroth in New York died from cyanide in Extra Strength Tylenol capsules. The cyanide was chemically different, but a tampered bottle near the purchase site matched it. Eight states banned capsules within five days.

segments.title: Scott Bartos self-published book
segments.summary: A former Johnson & Johnson employee, Scott Bartos, wrote a 2011 self-published book alleging the company knew the poison was in its distribution network and covered it up.

segments.title: Episode wrap-up
segments.summary: Josh sums up the Tylenol poisonings as a change for America and suggests listeners research more.

segments.title: Listener mail: synthetic farts
segments.summary: A listener from Brunswick, Maine recounts a college prank using a product called liquid ass, which she bought in high school, that fouled a dorm floor. The hosts react.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh asks for listener college prank stories and gives contact info; closing credits.
